newsitem.title: HUNGARY: TRACTEBEL, EDF STILL SEEKING PROMISED HUNGARY PROFIT.
newsitem.headline: TRACTEBEL, EDF STILL SEEKING PROMISED HUNGARY PROFIT.

text.p: West European energy companies utilities Tractebel and Electricite de France have expressed dissatisfaction at the slow pace of talks with Hungarian government officials aimed at resolving differences over future energy price mechanisms.

"The negotiations are becoming glutinous," Tractebel's representative in Hungary Tibor Kuhl told Reuters. "Within the framework of the power purchase agreements and price revision procedures, nothing has been settled...I can't tell you I'm very happy."

Tractebel, which bought 48 percent of the oil-fired Dunamenti power station in December 1995, is negotiating with APV over the price it is to receive for the power the plant supplies to Hungary's electricity company MVM, which sells on the electricity to the regional distributors.

Other Western utilities such as Electricite de France (EdF), Gaz de France and German electricity giant RWE have bought large stakes in the energy distribution sector and all new investors were promised an eight percent return on investment.

However all believe that by cancelling planned price rises in October last year and by fixing January energy price rises which still did not secure the expected margins the government had contravened the sales agreements it signed when they bought into the sector late in 1995.

"We are continuing not to get the promised profit," said Pierre Abou, representative in Hungary of EDF, which has just under 50 percent stakes in two regional electricity distribution companies, Edasz and Demasz.
"The formula is still valid but we disagree on the implementation -- these are technical questions and this is the reason it's taking so long."

Tractebel announced in January it was preparing legal action against the Hungarian government to recover its $141 million investment after the cancellation of the October price rise and Kuhl said the company has still not ruled out the possibility.

"I can't exclude (court action)," he said. "It is about privatisation commitments and terms of reference as described in the offering memorandum which were not respected in October last year...but it is a different issue from what we are discussing now."

Abou said the Western utilities had been pushing since January for the inclusion in the energy pricing formula of costs such as environmental safeguards, insurance, social payments and depreciation but had failed to persuade the Hungarian Energy Office (MEH) to incorporate any of them.
MEH announced a 3.6 percent quarterly rise for April 1 which took into account only the devaluation of the forint in the first three months.
Abou said he was looking for something more in the June 1 price adjustment and said EDF would reconsider its position on future investments if no progress had been made by then.
"If agreement is not reached before June we shall give them our precise standpoint," he said. "It is in our common interest to have this problem solved by the end of the quarter."

Kuhl also suggested there needed to be a clearer picture on profitability within the next few months and said that by the third quarter Tractebel will be making calculations as to whether their planned investment programme can go ahead.
"1997 is a test case on whether this investment is profitable or not." he said.
"The 1997 results are being monitored month by month and if it is proving that the 1997 results are accepteble then we will come to the conclusion that the tariff adjustement is also acceptable.
"(But) I'm not sure that the guaranteed return on equity will be achieved."

However, he said an agreement to allow Tractebel to pass on changes in heavy oil market prices meant the company would not incur the huge losses accumulated on the Dunamenti operation last year, when it bought oil from Hungarian oil company MOL at market rates but sold electricity to MVM at a fixed price.
"The tariff structure in 1997 is much less unpredictable than was the case in 1996 so there is already the possibility for planning the year and forecasting a certain level of profit."

Under new the mechanism the government continues to set the producer price but there is an additional compensation fee which can be either plus or minus according how the market price for MOL oil has moved, Kuhl said.
